title: system tests: podman healthcheck flaky, the unhealthy event fires just before the --since window opens
body:
Seen 28 times between 2026-06-04 and 2026-07-30, on both root and rootless, across fedora-prior, fedora-current, rawhide and debian-sid. Almost always the same message.

```
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6873471Z # [17:31:57.282179556] $ podman exec c-h-t212-ioqzhhpk touch /uh-oh
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6882867Z # [17:32:00.356398465] {"Status":"healthy","FailingStreak":2,"Log":[{...,"ExitCode":0},{...,"ExitCode":0},{...,"ExitCode":1},{...,"ExitCode":1}]}
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6885668Z #   libpod-conmon-caa2b7d2b2e8816ca617567f027cf592d28c5073feacb67d110a7796ffd6db27.scope      loaded    active running
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6888941Z #   caa2b7d2b2e8816ca617567f027cf592d28c5073feacb67d110a7796ffd6db27-4d5f2e5e0f0173c3.service loaded    active running
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6894234Z #   caa2b7d2b2e8816ca617567f027cf592d28c5073feacb67d110a7796ffd6db27-4d5f2e5e0f0173c3.timer   loaded    active running
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6898492Z # [17:32:00.496967228] $ podman events --filter container=c-h-t212-ioqzhhpk --filter event=health_status --since 2026-07-20T17:32:00,418209571+00:00
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6900599Z # [17:32:01.637147059] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6902498Z # [17:32:02.902910416] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6904381Z # [17:32:04.294679524] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6906274Z # [17:32:05.367194016] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6916441Z # [17:32:06.851256665] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6918509Z # [17:32:09.634674809] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6920611Z # [17:32:10.790602038] $ podman events ...
2026-07-20T17:35:23.6922359Z # #| FAIL: Four or more failures - timed out waiting for 'unhealthy' in podman events
```

https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/29762279833/job/88421964442

A few more: [07-22](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/29951636314/job/89032377003), [07-21](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/29804524375/job/88658986341), [07-08](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/28966758980/job/85953987802), [06-24](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/28107803418/job/83228584233).

I first assumed the 5s in `_check_health` was too short, but that is not it - the loop also runs `podman events` each iteration so it actually waited 10.3s here, and 13.7s in another job. What I cannot explain is the middle of that block: `FailingStreak` sits at 2 with the timer still `active running`, and with `--health-interval 1s` nothing new is recorded for ten seconds. I measured the interval elsewhere in these logs and it is fine, median 1.10s.

Is the healthcheck service expected to keep running after the check starts exiting non-zero? I have only the macOS client here so I could not reproduce it locally.

hey Pual, I hit this again today on an PR, so it is still going on and on.

```

```

https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/actions/runs/30463622001/job/91203565547

`sys local rootless debian-sid`, same wording as the ones above had.

I have submitted a fix for this in #29374. 

`_check_health` in `test/system/220-healthcheck.bats` previously used a tight 5s timeout (8s when parallel). Under heavy parallel CI load, systemd timers for container healthchecks require longer to execute 3 retries, causing false-positive timeouts while `FailingStreak` is at 2. 

The PR increases the timeout window for `$CI` / `$PARALLEL_JOBSLOT` runs to prevent these intermittent timeouts.

@Luap99 rechecked against the journal artifacts, you were right and my title is wrong.

The streak does not stop at 2. Job 88658986341, container `c-h-t212-8z85pryk`, from `journal-sys-local-root-fedora-prior.log`:

```
14:29:15.412347871  healthy    streak=0
14:29:15.656128707  healthy    streak=0
14:29:16.518557451  healthy    streak=1
14:29:19.010015971  healthy    streak=2
14:29:20.897162043  unhealthy  streak=3
```

and the `--since` that `_check_health` polls with in that job is `2026-07-21T14:29:20,916284157`, so the window opens 19 ms after the event it is waiting for.

Same shape on job 89032377003, container `c-h-t212-cboduw61`: unhealthy at `19:56:46.344191789`, and the last `--since` is `19:56:46,404004262`, 60 ms late.

So the 8 to 14 s of polling that follows cannot succeed however long it runs, and raising the timeout would not change that. I will fix the title.

Looking at createTimer in libpod/healthcheck_linux.go, the healthcheck timer is scheduled with --on-unit-inactive, so each run's interval is relative to when the previous run's transient unit exits, not a fixed wall-clock cadence. System tests run via bats -j $(nproc) (Makefile) on an 8-vCPU runner, so up to 8 test files execute fully in parallel with no spare core capacity — which is presumably why _check_health already has a load-aware timeout margin for PARALLEL_JOBSLOT. I don't see any concurrent podman command against this specific container between the "first failure" and "four or more failures" checks (just systemctl queries, which shouldn't touch the container lock), so my guess is a CPU-starved healthcheck run under that 8-way parallel load delays its own process exit — and because the next interval doesn't start counting until that exit, one starved run produces a full ~10s stall rather than gradual drift. Would it make sense to make the timer interval wall-clock-based (e.g. OnCalendar or absolute scheduling) instead of relative to previous-unit-exit, or is that tradeoff intentional? Happy to dig further if useful.

@TanayJalan the ~10s stall was my misreading, corrected above so there is no stall for wall-clock scheduling to fix - what fails is on the test side, the --since is captured after the unhealthy event fires, so the events window can never contain it however the timer is scheduled.

> [@TanayJalan](https://github.com/TanayJalan) the ~10s stall was my misreading, corrected above so there is no stall for wall-clock scheduling to fix - what fails is on the test side, the --since is captured after the unhealthy event fires, so the events window can never contain it however the timer is scheduled.

@vtushar06 Thanks, traced it through the actual test now. The race is even tighter than I first thought: _check_health "First failure" (lines 92–97) reads FailingStreak via inspect, accepting any value in [123] in the failing run this shows FailingStreak: 2. Right after that, line 101 re-captures current_time for the next --since, with a comment saying it's there specifically to avoid missing the unhealthy event during the systemctl checks that follow. But since FailingStreak is already 2 when that re-capture happens, only one more failing check is needed to flip to unhealthy and that can fire in the gap between the inspect read and the date call on line 101 (about 62ms in the actual log). So the existing mitigation doesn't cover the one race that actually matters. Would it make sense to just drop the re-capture on line 101 and reuse the original current_time from line 88 (before the failure was even forced) for both checks? That removes the gap entirely since --since would predate every possible transition. Happy to put up a PR for that if it looks right.
